title: Opportunities for Odor: Experiences with Smell and Implications for Technology
central_proposition: This paper investigates personal memorable smell experiences and their associated emotions to understand how emerging smell technologies can better match human experiences, proposing 10 categories of smell experience and exploring their implications for technology design.

concept_definitions.name: Smell stories
concept_definitions.definition: descriptions of personal memorable experiences involving smell

argument_structure: The argument is built by collecting 439 personal smell stories through an online questionnaire, systematically categorizing these stories into 10 main categories and 36 sub-categories based on experiential, emotional, and smell qualities. The implications for technology design are then explored through participant feedback and HCI researcher brainstorming, leading to discussions on how findings can benefit research on personal memories, momentary experiences, and wellbeing.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Smell plays a powerful role in connecting humans to past events and experiences by evoking older, more emotionally loaded, and vivid autobiographical memories. It influences mood changes, stimulates action, creates expectations, and supports behavioral/attitudinal shifts, often based on associative learning. Smells can also be invasive, overwhelming, and affect social interaction.

findings.antecedent: Smell encountered during a special past event (e.g., 'Wedding Day', 'Grandma's House', 'Christmas Eve')
findings.consequent: Strong association to those particular past moments, positive experiences (n=127), negative experiences (n=27)
findings.mechanism: Smell acts as a strong associative cue for past events, binding them to memory.
findings.source: Category 1: Associating the past with a smell
findings.quote: In these stories the smell was described as having a strong association to those particular moments in the past

findings.antecedent: Recent experience of a smell (present stimulus)
findings.consequent: Reminded participants about past events, people, locations, or specific times (indirect link), mainly positive experiences (n=37)
findings.mechanism: A present smell stimulus acts as an indirect cue for past memories, causing a flashback.
findings.source: Category 2: Remembering through a smell
findings.quote: Most stories in this category contain reminders of childhood described as 'sweet', 'reassuring' and 'nostalgic'

findings.antecedent: Unique, mostly unknown smell (e.g., 'first time' encounters with food, nature, perfume)
findings.consequent: Perceived as stimulating, positive experience (all but one story), mixed attributes (e.g., heavy, imitating, stimulating)
findings.mechanism: Novel or unique smells can be perceived as stimulating, leading to positive experiences, even with mixed attributes.
findings.source: Category 3: Smell perceived as stimulating
findings.quote: The 62 stories in this category described experiences with a unique, mostly unknown smell

findings.antecedent: Smell (associated with food, nature, other people's scent, newness)
findings.consequent: Grabbed attention unexpectedly, motivated action/desire (e.g., appetite, curiosity, attractiveness), stimulated reflection (one story), 45 positive experiences
findings.mechanism: Smell acts as an unexpected attentional cue that can trigger approach behaviors or cognitive processes like reflection, even in negative situations.
findings.source: Category 4: Smell creating desire for more
findings.quote: Key to these stories is that the smell grabbed the persons' attention unexpectedly.

findings.antecedent: Smell (e.g., 'Gas leak')
findings.consequent: Enabled identification/detection of a situation, allowed participant to act or prevent something, emotions like anxious, conscientious, confident, serious
findings.mechanism: Smell provides immediate, salient information for threat detection and rapid action.
findings.source: Category 5: Smell allowing identification and detection
findings.quote: This category captures the enabling role of smell in certain situations, such as allowing one to identify or detect a smell

findings.antecedent: Smell (disturbing, sudden, during activity, e.g., 'The Smell of Death', 'local county jail')
findings.consequent: Overwhelmed the person, traumatizing, vivid memory of the smell itself (not the event), desire to forget the smell, predominantly negative experiences (n=30)
findings.mechanism: Intense, unpleasant smells can bypass cognitive control, leading to strong, persistent negative emotional and sensory experiences, distinct from memory associations.
findings.source: Category 6: Overwhelming power of smell
findings.quote: This category includes 37 stories where the smell overwhelmed the person in a positive way (n = 5) but predominately in a negative way (n = 30)

findings.antecedent: Lingering smell (e.g., 'Don't want to smell that twice!', 'skunk')
findings.consequent: Inability to get rid of the smell, smell invades personal/public space, loss of control, forced to leave space, mainly negative experiences
findings.mechanism: Persistent, unpleasant smells can violate personal space boundaries, leading to discomfort and a sense of lost control.
findings.source: Category 7: Smell invading private and public spaces
findings.quote: The smell invaded private and public spaces. In contrast to the previous category, the smell entered the person's personal space

findings.antecedent: Person's own smell or smell of others (e.g., 'Dragon breath teacher')
findings.consequent: Negatively affected social interaction, togetherness, embarrassment, discomfort, overall negative experiences
findings.mechanism: Unpleasant body odors can create social discomfort, impede communication, and trigger negative emotional responses in social interactions.
findings.source: Category 8: Social interaction is affected by the smell
findings.quote: Smell negatively affected the interaction among people and their togetherness

findings.antecedent: Smell (e.g., 'White Lilac Sheets' for divorce, 'Accidental vegetarian')
findings.consequent: Changes mood, attitude, or behavior; active regulating effect on mood, mainly positive experiences (n=12)
findings.mechanism: Smells can directly influence emotional states and cognitive appraisals, leading to shifts in mood, attitude, and subsequent behavior.
findings.source: Category 9: Smell changes mood, attitude and behavior
findings.quote: This category contains 23 stories, which underlined the power of smells to change a person's mood, attitude, or behavior.

findings.antecedent: Smell (e.g., 'The Smell of Hungry Anticipation' with rosemary, 'PomVinegar Surprise')
findings.consequent: Builds up expectations, creates surprise by exceeding anticipations, enhances momentary experiences, positive experiences
findings.mechanism: Smell can act as a powerful cue to generate predictions about future sensory experiences, and violations of these predictions can lead to surprise.
findings.source: Category 10: Smell builds up and changes expectations
findings.quote: This category shows the potential of smell to build up expectations and to surprise.

findings.antecedent: Smell of special moments (newborn baby), personal database smells
findings.consequent: Remote participation in family events, sharing understanding, designing/sharing new smells
findings.mechanism: Capturing and transmitting smells allows for shared sensory experiences across distance, enhancing social connection and memory recall.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from participants
findings.quote: To share smells with family/friends: allow one to participate in a family event through remote smelling

findings.antecedent: Smell-enhanced online shopping, smell profiles for holiday places/travel, smell matchmaker for dating
findings.consequent: Quick judgment (like/dislike), better decision making
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues provide rapid, implicit evaluative information that aids in decision-making.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from participants
findings.quote: To support decision making: use smells for a quick judgment in online shopping

findings.antecedent: Smell (from good experiences, calming scents)
findings.consequent: Relive good experiences, get in better mood, calm down in stressful moments, cheer up when depressed
findings.mechanism: Smells can trigger emotionally potent memories or directly influence mood states.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from participants
findings.quote: To regulate mood actively/passively: smell to relive good experiences whenever you want to get in a better mood

findings.antecedent: Smell integrated into radio, music apps, TV ads, concerts, theater, underwater diving
findings.consequent: Enhanced experiences
findings.mechanism: Multisensory congruence and enrichment can heighten engagement and immersion in various activities.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from participants
findings.quote: To combine with other technologies and activities: integrate smell into radio

findings.antecedent: Smell-enhanced wristband, glasses, jewelry, clothes
findings.consequent: Preferred perfume lingering, seeing/smelling the beach, wedding ring enhanced with smell
findings.mechanism: Integrating smell into personal objects can create continuous, personalized sensory cues that evoke memories or desired states.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from participants
findings.quote: To combine with everyday objects: enhance wristband with smell for keeping a preferred perfume lingering

findings.antecedent: Technology for body smell detection
findings.consequent: Avoid embarrassing moments, provide invisible cues about smell level, quick smell check after sporting activities
findings.mechanism: Real-time olfactory feedback can help individuals manage social perceptions and personal hygiene.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from participants
findings.quote: To make oneself and others aware about body smell: to avoid embarrassing moments

findings.antecedent: Technology stimulating smell (e.g., different smells to avoid habituation)
findings.consequent: Structure the day, take activities/moods into account, reminder to take a break, motivation to keep going
findings.mechanism: Smells can influence mood and cognitive states, acting as cues for behavior regulation and motivation.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from HCI researchers
findings.quote: Smell-enhanced performance regulator: a technology stimulating smell in order to structure the day

findings.antecedent: Robot spreading ambient cues, smell trails in the environment
findings.consequent: Guide someone to a place, build up expectations, motivate action, make hidden information accessible (e.g., warning about tense working atmosphere)
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues can provide spatial and contextual information, influencing navigation, expectations, and behavior.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from HCI researchers
findings.quote: Autonomous smell agent: a technology spreading ambient cues (e.g., a robot) to guide someone to a certain place

findings.antecedent: Pleasant or critical bad smells as reminders
findings.consequent: Remind about important events (birthdays, appointments), not easily ignored
findings.mechanism: Smells are powerful, less ignorable cues than visual/auditory, especially unpleasant ones, for critical reminders.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from HCI researchers
findings.quote: Reminder alert with smell: a technology to remind us about important events, birthdays, and appointments.

findings.antecedent: Digitized incense stick with layers of smells related to a loved person, new smells added by friends/family
findings.consequent: Stimulates storytelling, triggers new stories about dead person, anchor points for memory
findings.mechanism: Smells act as potent memory cues, facilitating narrative recall and shared social experiences.
findings.source: Ideas for technology from HCI researchers
findings.quote: Smell-enhanced storytelling: a technology that stimulates storytelling around a digitized version of an incense stick.

findings.antecedent: Negative smell stories (n=112)
findings.consequent: Slightly longer story length (M=90 words) than positive stories (M=79 words)
findings.mechanism: Negative experiences may prompt more detailed or elaborate descriptions.
findings.source: Key quantitative facts behind the smell stories
findings.quote: negative stories tended to be slightly longer (M = 90 words) than positive stories (M = 79 words), but the difference is statistically not significant

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The power of smell to evoke memories and emotions will diminish if smells are always available, suggesting that restricted access or specific social settings can preserve their uniqueness.
Designing reminder systems that use escalating unpleasant smells (starting pleasant, turning unpleasant if ignored) will be more effective than purely pleasant or purely visual/auditory reminders.
Integrating smells with technologies for personal memories (e.g., photos, videos) will enrich the user experience and aid in memory recall for individuals with memory loss.
Smell-enhanced technologies can be a valuable research strategy in wellbeing research by leveraging the positive emotional impact of smells for mood regulation.
bridge_warrants: The findings on smell and personal memories (Categories 1 & 2) can enrich research on memory loss (e.g., dementia), life-logging tools, and end-of-life technologies.

The insights into in-situ smell stimulation, capture, and sharing (Categories 3-8, 10) are relevant for real-time smell-enhanced technologies like mobile phones, photo/video cameras, and website navigation.
The exploration of bad smells (Categories 6-8) can inform the design of novel reminder systems, potentially using escalating unpleasantness.
The understanding of smell's role in mood, attitude, and behavior change (Category 9) can be applied to wellbeing and behavior change research, such as healthy nutrition and positive psychology.
methodological_critiques: Existing HCI work on smell technologies primarily focuses on development and evaluation of smell perception of single stimuli, lacking insight into the subjective experience of smell.
There is a lack of knowledge pertaining to the description and classification of smells required for HCI, leading to arbitrary smell usage in previous systems.
limitations: The study's participants were limited to the US, potentially limiting the generalizability of smell stories due to cultural and geographical differences.
Collecting narratives via an online questionnaire limited the depth of exploration compared to interview situations.
The study provides an overview of an emerging field, and future in-depth research inspired by the identified categories is needed.
